title: Inside John Mack's Strategy to Save Morgan Stanley
description: Oct. 8  -- Former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke and Former Morgan Stanley Chairman and CEO John Mack discuss the 2008 financial crisis. They speak on "Bloomberg ‹GO›."  -- Subscribe to Bloomberg on YouTube: http://www.youtube.com/Bloomberg  Bloomberg Television offers extensive coverage and analysis of international business news and stories of global importance. It is available in more than 310 million households worldwide and reaches the most affluent and influential viewers in terms of household income, asset value and education levels. With production hubs in London, New York and Hong Kong, the network provides 24-hour continuous coverage of the people, companies and ideas that move the markets.

asr.full_text: In the conversation that he had, and Hank Paulsen and Guyton and I had was a very forceful conversation on what they wanted Morgan Stanley to do which as he remembers, I was not going to do that And what do they want you to do? They want us sell the firm for $2 a share And to sell it to? JP Morgan in all fairness, it was Tim who wanted that Yeah, I wasn't on the conversation It was Tim, in all fairness And was Tim who wanted that. I don't know where. Yeah. I wasn't on that conversation. It was Tim, in all fairness. And was Jamie Dimon interested? Would he have bought it at that? He was not interested and he said, All I pay you is two dollars a share. No. We have three or four conversations that Tim kept saying, Call Jamie and that Jamie didn't want to do it. And I didn't want to do it. But when the head of New York Fed is pushing you to make those calls you make the calls. So after the fact when we look at the last few years and the problems banks have faced since these acquisitions. Is it fair because when we look and say well it was the Fed who pushed the bank and push the banks into into these trades one would say no that's not fair. Yeah you're talking about to get us in this position? No the street look. When you just make money and the markets going your way and you can borrow low, sell high, you can securitize and people are making 20, 30% in ROEs with their stock, someone's got to blow the whistle. It got carried away and and leverage was wild. I mean when you think about the leverage these firms had including Morgan Stanley And leverage was wild. When you think about the leverage these firms had, including Morgan Stanley, it was absurd. But when everything is going up, everyone wants to play. I remember calling Tim on a leverage loan deal we were trying to make. We were uncomfortable with it. We kept passing. Finally, our guy said, look, we have to be involved. We passed on the last three deals. We get involved at 6 times leverage which is ridiculous. And then once the sponsor had the leverage they turned it over to 7 times leverage. We dropped out, I called the head of the New York Fed and said were out of control. Said I can say no to 1, 2 maybe 3 deals. On the fourth deal, I have to play. So, you knew Morgan Stanley was over-leveraged. Did you know that they were over-leveraged? Only a fool could have not known that we were all over-leveraged. but the Fed must've seen that. Did the Fed see that? Well, it was becoming increasingly obvious, as we got into the crisis, but part of it was happening is that with the fear and the panic, people were dumping securities quickly as possible and that was driving down the prices prices and was causing the situation to get worse. Today when you look at what corporate America is doing, we are seeing corporations borrow trillions of dollars to buy back stock, we are seeing M&A at record levels, is that helping the economy? Are we really... It can't help. It can't help. It can? Sure. Of course it can. First of all, the buybacks... How does this level of buybacks help? Buybacks put money in the economy. It gives the shareholders money. The M&A, if it's good M&A, is going to... If it's good M&A, it'll improve efficiency and rationalize markets. And you think that's what we have right now? In some cases, I don't know. But where is leverage today compared to where it was in 2007? It's not anywhere close to that. That was my sense. It is not even close. There has been very huge leverage. Any bank corporations. There has been, but also you have to remember the regulators now are much more pro-active not just with the CFO or the CEO, with boards. Regulators are coming in into board meetings talking about risk talking about leverage. That didn't happen. Eight years ago. Seven years ago. Yeah this happening now. This is a fascinating thing that I had not realized that we actually have representatives of the Fed who are sitting in board meetings and banks. Now more than that you actually have a representative the feds sitting in the building. I'm going to guess. Morgan Stanley has one hundred and fifty to two hundred people there who live in all the bank. Yeah absolutely. And you're not concerned as we're seeing like in the leveraged loan market for example. Covenant Like coming back in the universe like this makes me feel a little bit anxious when you look at high yield and distress again unsophisticated investors being pushed into those markets. What happens when rates normalize. Well look I think again you need to look at their balance sheet and the balance sheet today are conservative they could handle that kind of stress right now thanks can't yes can investors you've got insurance companies well being pushed because about rates are into riskier assets what happens we had this rate hike not be back holding the bag it could be investors well investors have to you know the Fed is not in charge of making sure investors make money and his fed is in charge of making sure the financial stability is preserved. So the Fed is looking at all these financial conditions and trying to think about what could happen. What are the risks and the concern the Fed has is not that somebody loses money. The concern that Fed has is that because of leverage or other reasons, the loss of money leads to instability in the system and that's the concern. But those investors, for example, are insurance companies. Those are state pensions being pushed– Well, they have regulators, too. They have regulators, too. And, given where rates are, they have been pushed into further, and further riskier assets. And while banks can't take on risk anymore, the high-yield market has frozen. It makes me very concerned for those investors. We're just moving where the risk is sitting. I think you're overly concerned. I really do. I don't know what the time frame on this discussion is, but I want to say something very clearly. I've said it to Hank, and I've said it again, but I want to say it on air. The two heroes is this gentleman and Hank Paulson. Their leadership, and look, I didn't agree with them, and I was really upset with them when they were trying to break my arm to sell the firm at sorry we got through it they did their job we did our job but their leadership that's what saved
